title: Safety Filters, PII in Traces, Bias, Content Safety & Monitoring
scopeHtml: Scope: Validating inputs/outputs, keeping PII out of logs, bias testing, harmful-output detection, alerts for production failures.

notes.title: The safety pipeline as layers of filters
notes.html:
What it is. A safety filter is a small piece of code (or a small model) that sits between two things and decides: pass, change, or block. In a GenAI app there are four natural places to put one: before the model sees the user message (input filter), before the model's answer reaches the user (output filter), before a tool call runs (action filter), and on the data you write to logs (trace filter). The rest of these notes walk through each place plus the two things that keep it honest over time: bias measurement and monitoring.

Why it exists. A language model (an LLM, a program that predicts the next token, a token being a word fragment) is not a deterministic function. The same input can give different outputs, and users and web pages can feed it hostile text. You cannot unit-test every possible conversation, so you wrap the model in cheap deterministic checks that catch the common, expensive failures.

How it works, step by step.

user text
   |
   v
[1 INPUT FILTER]  length, encoding, PII, injection patterns, topic, moderation
   |  block -> canned refusal (model never called, cost = 0)
   v
[ MODEL + TOOLS ]  <-- [3 ACTION FILTER] allow-list, argument checks, approval
   |
   v
[2 OUTPUT FILTER]  schema, secrets, PII, harm classifier, groundedness
   |  block -> safe fallback message
   v
user sees answer

every stage also emits:
[4 TRACE FILTER]  redact PII, then write span to the observability backend
                  -> metrics -> dashboards -> alerts

Design rules that matter more than any single check:

  1. Order cheap before expensive. Regex and length checks cost microseconds, a moderation model costs tens to hundreds of milliseconds (verify for your provider), the main model costs seconds. Reject early.
  2. Decide per check whether failure is fail-open (let the request through) or fail-closed (block). A crashed PII scanner on a medical app should fail closed. A crashed "tone" classifier on a casual chat app may fail open. Write the choice down.
  3. Return a reason code from every filter (for example INPUT_TOO_LONG, PII_EMAIL). Reason codes become your metrics later.
  4. Filters reduce risk, they never remove it. Every filter has false positives (good request blocked) and false negatives (bad request passed). You tune the trade-off, you never reach zero on both.

Real products. OpenAI ships a moderation endpoint (verify current model names in the docs), Meta published Llama Guard as an open safety classifier model, NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails and Guardrails AI are open source frameworks that run input and output rails, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails and Azure AI Content Safety are managed versions. Anthropic's API offers system prompts and models trained to refuse, and many teams add a small classifier model such as a fast tier model (for example claude-haiku-5-5, verify) as a judge on top.

Everyday analogy (after the explanation). An airport. Ticket check, ID check, bag scanner, gate check: each is cheap and imperfect, the stack together is strong, and the order is arranged so the quick checks happen first. See also in 02_S1: "Input and output guardrails" for the full catalogue of guardrails; this note goes deeper on implementation, logging, measurement and alerting.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "we added a moderation API so we are safe". It is one layer, with false negatives, and it does nothing for PII in logs or tool misuse.
  • Forgetting the fail-open vs fail-closed decision. Interviewers like "what happens when your filter times out?".
  • Blocking only on the input. Indirect attacks arrive through retrieved documents and tool results, so you must filter what enters the context too, and the output.
  • Treating the filter's own prompt as secure. An LLM-based filter can itself be prompt-injected, so keep its verdict a strict label (safe/unsafe) and parse it, never act on free text.

notes.title: Validating inputs in code
notes.html:
What it is. Input validation is everything you check on user (and retrieved) text before it reaches the model.

Why. Three reasons: cost (a 2 MB paste is a denial-of-wallet attack: you pay per token), safety (obvious attack strings, hidden characters) and privacy (do not send raw card numbers to a third party).

Checks, in order.

  1. Size: limit characters and estimated tokens. A rough rule for English is about 4 characters per token, so 8,000 characters is about 2,000 tokens. That is an estimate, use the provider token counter for exact numbers (verify the SDK method).
  2. Normalise Unicode: apply NFKC normalisation so full-width and look-alike characters collapse, and strip zero-width and control characters. Attackers hide instructions with zero-width spaces (U+200B) and "tag" characters.
  3. Pattern screens: a short list of known injection phrases ("ignore previous instructions"). This catches lazy attacks only. It is a speed bump, say so in interviews.
  4. PII detection: emails, phone numbers, card numbers (verify with the Luhn checksum to cut false positives), national IDs.
  5. Topic or scope: is this a question a support bot should answer?
  6. Optional moderation model call.

Luhn in one line of reasoning: from the right, double every second digit, subtract 9 if the result is above 9, sum all; valid if the sum mod 10 is 0. Example 4242 4242 4242 4242 is the well known test card and passes. A random 16-digit order number passes only 1 time in 10, so Luhn removes about 90 percent of false hits.

import re, unicodedata

MAX_CHARS = 8000
ZERO_WIDTH = dict.fromkeys(map(ord, "​‌‍⁠﻿"), None)
INJECTION = re.compile(r"ignore (all )?(previous|prior) instructions|reveal (your )?system prompt", re.I)

def luhn_ok(digits: str) -> bool:
    total, flip = 0, False
    for ch in reversed(digits):
        d = int(ch)
        if flip:
            d = d * 2 - 9 if d * 2 > 9 else d * 2
        total += d
        flip = not flip
    return total % 10 == 0

def validate_input(text: str):
    """Returns (clean_text, reason_code or None)."""
    if len(text) > MAX_CHARS:
        return text, "INPUT_TOO_LONG"
    clean = unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", text).translate(ZERO_WIDTH)
    if INJECTION.search(clean):
        return clean, "INJECTION_PATTERN"
    for m in re.finditer(r"\b(?:\d[ -]?){13,16}\b", clean):
        if luhn_ok(re.sub(r"\D", "", m.group())):
            return clean, "PII_CARD"
    return clean, None

print(validate_input("Please ignore previous instructions"))  # ('Please ignore previous instructions', 'INJECTION_PATTERN')
import java.text.Normalizer

const val MAX_CHARS = 8000
val ZERO_WIDTH = Regex("[\\u200b\\u200c\\u200d\\u2060\\ufeff]")
val INJECTION = Regex("ignore (all )?(previous|prior) instructions|reveal (your )?system prompt", RegexOption.IGNORE_CASE)
val CARD = Regex("\\b(?:\\d[ -]?){13,16}\\b")

fun luhnOk(digits: String): Boolean {
    var sum = 0
    var flip = false
    for (ch in digits.reversed()) {
        var d = ch - '0'
        if (flip) { d *= 2; if (d > 9) d -= 9 }
        sum += d
        flip = !flip
    }
    return sum % 10 == 0
}

// returns Pair(cleanText, reasonCode or null)
fun validateInput(text: String): Pair<String, String?> {
    if (text.length > MAX_CHARS) return text to "INPUT_TOO_LONG"
    val clean = Normalizer.normalize(text, Normalizer.Form.NFKC).replace(ZERO_WIDTH, "")
    if (INJECTION.containsMatchIn(clean)) return clean to "INJECTION_PATTERN"
    for (m in CARD.findAll(clean)) {
        if (luhnOk(m.value.filter { it.isDigit() })) return clean to "PII_CARD"
    }
    return clean to null
}
import java.text.Normalizer;
import java.util.regex.*;

public class InputFilter {
    static final int MAX_CHARS = 8000;
    static final Pattern ZERO_WIDTH = Pattern.compile("[\\u200b\\u200c\\u200d\\u2060\\ufeff]");
    static final Pattern INJECTION = Pattern.compile(
        "ignore (all )?(previous|prior) instructions|reveal (your )?system prompt", Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE);
    static final Pattern CARD = Pattern.compile("\\b(?:\\d[ -]?){13,16}\\b");

    static boolean luhnOk(String digits) {
        int sum = 0; boolean flip = false;
        for (int i = digits.length() - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
            int d = digits.charAt(i) - '0';
            if (flip) { d *= 2; if (d > 9) d -= 9; }
            sum += d; flip = !flip;
        }
        return sum % 10 == 0;
    }

    /** Returns the reason code, or null when the input passes. */
    static String validate(String text) {
        if (text.length() > MAX_CHARS) return "INPUT_TOO_LONG";
        String clean = ZERO_WIDTH.matcher(Normalizer.normalize(text, Normalizer.Form.NFKC)).replaceAll("");
        if (INJECTION.matcher(clean).find()) return "INJECTION_PATTERN";
        Matcher m = CARD.matcher(clean);
        while (m.find()) if (luhnOk(m.group().replaceAll("\\D", ""))) return "PII_CARD";
        return null;
    }
}

Real products. Microsoft Presidio is an open source PII detector and anonymiser; Google Cloud DLP and AWS Comprehend PII do the same as managed services; Lakera Guard and Rebuff style tools detect injection (verify current status of any named product).

Everyday analogy. A mailroom that weighs every parcel, x-rays it, and refuses anything leaking liquid before it enters the building.

Common interview traps.

  • Relying on a phrase blocklist as the injection defence. It is trivially bypassed with other languages, base64 or paraphrase, so layer it under least-privilege tools.
  • Counting characters instead of tokens for cost, and ignoring that non-English text uses more tokens per character.
  • Forgetting to validate retrieved documents and tool outputs, which are also "input".
  • Running regexes with catastrophic backtracking on attacker-controlled text (ReDoS). Keep patterns simple and bound the length first.

notes.title: Validating outputs in code
notes.html:
What it is. Output validation checks the model's answer before a human or another system consumes it.

Why. The model can leak secrets that were in its context, produce malformed JSON that crashes your parser, emit markdown or HTML that executes in a browser (XSS, cross-site scripting), or say something harmful. Output is untrusted data, exactly like a form field typed by a stranger.

Checks.

  1. Structure: if you asked for JSON, parse it and validate against a schema (JSON Schema, Pydantic, kotlinx.serialization, Jackson). On failure retry once with the error message, then fall back.
  2. Secrets: scan for key shapes (for example sk-, AKIA followed by 16 characters for AWS access keys, private key headers). Treat any hit as a security incident, not just a block.
  3. PII: the same detector as the input side, because the model can invent or recall personal data.
  4. Harm: a classifier (see the content safety section).
  5. Grounding for retrieval apps: each claim should be supported by a retrieved passage.
  6. Safe rendering: escape HTML, never eval or run generated SQL or shell with real privileges.
import json, re

SECRET = re.compile(r"AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}|-----BEGIN [A-Z ]*PRIVATE KEY-----|sk-[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}")
ALLOWED_ACTIONS = {"refund", "escalate", "answer"}

def validate_output(raw: str):
    """Expect JSON like {"action": "...", "text": "..."}; returns (obj or None, reason or None)."""
    if SECRET.search(raw):
        return None, "SECRET_LEAK"          # also page security
    try:
        obj = json.loads(raw)
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        return None, "BAD_JSON"
    if obj.get("action") not in ALLOWED_ACTIONS or not isinstance(obj.get("text"), str):
        return None, "BAD_SCHEMA"
    return obj, None

print(validate_output('{"action":"delete_all","text":"x"}'))  # (None, 'BAD_SCHEMA')
import kotlinx.serialization.*
import kotlinx.serialization.json.*

@Serializable data class Reply(val action: String, val text: String)

val SECRET = Regex("AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}|-----BEGIN [A-Z ]*PRIVATE KEY-----|sk-[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}")
val ALLOWED = setOf("refund", "escalate", "answer")

// returns Pair(reply or null, reason or null)
fun validateOutput(raw: String): Pair<Reply?, String?> {
    if (SECRET.containsMatchIn(raw)) return null to "SECRET_LEAK"
    val reply = try { Json.decodeFromString<Reply>(raw) } catch (e: SerializationException) { return null to "BAD_JSON" }
    if (reply.action !in ALLOWED) return null to "BAD_SCHEMA"
    return reply to null
}
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.*;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.regex.Pattern;

public class OutputFilter {
    static final Pattern SECRET = Pattern.compile(
        "AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}|-----BEGIN [A-Z ]*PRIVATE KEY-----|sk-[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}");
    static final Set<String> ALLOWED = Set.of("refund", "escalate", "answer");
    static final ObjectMapper MAPPER = new ObjectMapper();

    /** Returns null when valid, otherwise the reason code. */
    static String validate(String raw) {
        if (SECRET.matcher(raw).find()) return "SECRET_LEAK";
        try {
            JsonNode n = MAPPER.readTree(raw);
            if (!n.hasNonNull("action") || !ALLOWED.contains(n.get("action").asText())
                || !n.path("text").isTextual()) return "BAD_SCHEMA";
            return null;
        } catch (Exception e) {
            return "BAD_JSON";
        }
    }
}

An allow-list on action is the key idea: the model proposes, your code disposes. Even a fully jailbroken model cannot trigger delete_all if the executor refuses unknown actions.

Streaming wrinkle. Streaming sends tokens as they are generated, so you cannot validate the full answer first. Options: buffer a sentence or a few hundred milliseconds at a time and run cheap checks on the buffer; run the heavy classifier on the full text and retract (replace the message) if it fails; or do not stream for high-risk flows. State the trade-off: streaming improves perceived latency but weakens output blocking.

Everyday analogy. A proofreader who checks the printed page against the style guide before it leaves the print shop, and a cashier who only accepts items from the menu.

Common interview traps.

  • Validating JSON syntax but not values (a valid JSON with "amount": -5000).
  • Rendering model markdown straight into a WebView or HTML without escaping.
  • Running a classifier after the answer is already streamed to the user, then calling it a block.
  • Retrying validation failures without a cap, which turns a bad prompt into a cost loop.

notes.title: Why PII ends up in traces
notes.html:
What it is. A trace is a record of one request's journey through your system, made of spans (one span per step, such as "call model" or "retrieve documents") with attributes (key-value details). OpenTelemetry (OTel) is the standard format. LLM observability tools (Langfuse, LangSmith, Arize Phoenix, Helicone, and OTel-based setups; verify current names) record prompts, completions, tool arguments and retrieved text as span attributes because that is exactly what you need to debug a bad answer.

PII means personally identifiable information: names, emails, phone numbers, addresses, government IDs, card numbers, health data, precise location, and also combinations that identify someone indirectly.

Why the problem exists. The thing that makes LLM traces useful (full prompt and full answer) is the thing that makes them dangerous. In a classic web service you log an order id; in a GenAI service the "payload" is free text a human typed, so it can contain anything. A user pastes a bank statement into a support chat and now it sits in your log store.

Where PII leaks (the map).

user message ------------------> span attribute "prompt"        (log store)
retrieved chunks (CRM, docs) ---> span attribute "context"       (log store)
tool arguments/results --------> span attribute "tool.args"     (log store)
model answer ------------------> span attribute "completion"    (log store)
exception stack traces --------> error logs with message text   (log store)
HTTP request bodies in proxies -> access logs, APM agents       (vendor SaaS)
evaluation datasets built from prod traces -> shared notebooks, spreadsheets
prompt caches / semantic caches -> keyed by raw text

Real consequences: regulators (GDPR in the EU, CCPA in California, HIPAA for US health data; verify specifics with legal) treat logs as personal data stores, so a breach of the observability vendor is a breach of your users' data, and a "delete my data" request must reach logs too. Engineers with dashboard access see data they never should.

Real-world production failure patterns.

  • Debug flag left on: LOG_PROMPTS=true enabled during an incident and never turned off.
  • Third-party APM auto-instrumentation captures HTTP bodies of calls to the model provider without anyone configuring it.
  • A support engineer copies a "bad trace" into a ticket, and the PII spreads to the ticketing tool.
  • The model echoes PII in the answer, which is logged even though you scrubbed the input.
  • Android: the app logs the prompt with Log.d, readable via adb logcat on debuggable builds and by other tools on old devices; crash reporters such as Firebase Crashlytics attach custom keys and log lines, which then leave the device.

Everyday analogy. A hospital that photocopies every patient file "for quality review" and leaves the copies in an unlocked room.

Common interview traps.

  • "We hash the user id so logs are anonymous". Hashing a low-entropy value (phone number) is reversible by brute force, and a hashed id is still personal data if it can be linked back (pseudonymisation is not anonymisation).
  • Believing the model provider's no-training promise covers your own log store. It does not.
  • Scrubbing only the prompt and forgetting retrieved context, tool results and exceptions.
  • Thinking PII is only names and emails. Free-text medical details and addresses in sentences are PII too.

notes.title: Keeping PII out of traces in code
notes.html:
What it is. Redaction (replace with a placeholder like [EMAIL]) applied before the data is written to a span. Do it at one choke point so no engineer can forget.

Strategies, strongest first.

  1. Do not record the content at all. Record metadata: token counts, latency, model id, a request id, reason codes, hashed ids with a secret key (HMAC, not plain SHA).
  2. Record content only for a sampled slice (for example 1 percent) or only on failure, and redact it.
  3. Redact with a detector (regex for structured PII, an NER model such as Presidio for names and addresses) before export.
  4. Tokenise reversibly: replace alice@x.com with <EMAIL_1> and keep the mapping in a separate, access-controlled vault with a short TTL, so you can restore text for the user but the logs stay clean.
  5. Put redaction in the telemetry pipeline too (for example an OTel Collector processor; verify processor names in the OTel docs) as a second net.

A consistent placeholder per value (<EMAIL_1> every time the same email appears) keeps the trace debuggable: you can still see "the model repeated the same address twice".

import re, hmac, hashlib, os

PATTERNS = {
    "EMAIL": re.compile(r"[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.-]+"),
    "PHONE": re.compile(r"\+?\d[\d ()-]{8,14}\d"),
}
KEY = os.environ["TRACE_HMAC_KEY"].encode()   # secret, rotate it

def redact(text: str) -> str:
    seen: dict[str, str] = {}
    def sub(kind):
        def f(m):
            return seen.setdefault(m.group(), f"<{kind}_{len(seen) + 1}>")
        return f
    for kind, pat in PATTERNS.items():
        text = pat.sub(sub(kind), text)
    return text

def user_key(user_id: str) -> str:
    return hmac.new(KEY, user_id.encode(), hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()[:16]

# with OpenTelemetry (opentelemetry-api): span.set_attribute("llm.prompt", redact(prompt))
print(redact("mail bob@x.com or bob@x.com, call +91 98765 43210"))  # mail <EMAIL_1> or <EMAIL_1>, call <PHONE_2>
import javax.crypto.Mac
import javax.crypto.spec.SecretKeySpec

val PATTERNS = linkedMapOf(
    "EMAIL" to Regex("[\\w.+-]+@[\\w-]+\\.[\\w.-]+"),
    "PHONE" to Regex("\\+?\\d[\\d ()-]{8,14}\\d"),
)

fun redact(text: String): String {
    val seen = LinkedHashMap<String, String>()
    var out = text
    for ((kind, pat) in PATTERNS) {
        out = pat.replace(out) { m -> seen.getOrPut(m.value) { "<${kind}_${seen.size + 1}>" } }
    }
    return out
}

fun userKey(userId: String, secret: ByteArray): String {
    val mac = Mac.getInstance("HmacSHA256").apply { init(SecretKeySpec(secret, "HmacSHA256")) }
    return mac.doFinal(userId.toByteArray()).joinToString("") { "%02x".format(it) }.take(16)
}

// with OpenTelemetry Java API: span.setAttribute("llm.prompt", redact(prompt))
import javax.crypto.Mac;
import javax.crypto.spec.SecretKeySpec;
import java.util.*;
import java.util.regex.*;

public class TraceScrubber {
    static final Map<String, Pattern> PATTERNS = new LinkedHashMap<>();
    static {
        PATTERNS.put("EMAIL", Pattern.compile("[\\w.+-]+@[\\w-]+\\.[\\w.-]+"));
        PATTERNS.put("PHONE", Pattern.compile("\\+?\\d[\\d ()-]{8,14}\\d"));
    }

    static String redact(String text) {
        Map<String, String> seen = new HashMap<>();
        for (var e : PATTERNS.entrySet()) {
            Matcher m = e.getValue().matcher(text);
            StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
            while (m.find()) {
                String ph = seen.computeIfAbsent(m.group(), k -> "<" + e.getKey() + "_" + (seen.size() + 1) + ">");
                m.appendReplacement(sb, Matcher.quoteReplacement(ph));
            }
            m.appendTail(sb);
            text = sb.toString();
        }
        return text;
    }

    static String userKey(String userId, byte[] secret) throws Exception {
        Mac mac = Mac.getInstance("HmacSHA256");
        mac.init(new SecretKeySpec(secret, "HmacSHA256"));
        return HexFormat.of().formatHex(mac.doFinal(userId.getBytes())).substring(0, 16);
    }
    // with OpenTelemetry Java API: span.setAttribute("llm.prompt", redact(prompt));
}

Regex limits to state out loud: it misses names ("my name is Priya Nair"), addresses and anything non-standard; it also over-matches (a 10-digit order number looks like a phone). That is why high-risk apps add an NER model and sample-audit the redacted logs by hand.

Everyday analogy. A newspaper that blacks out names in court documents before printing, and keeps the key to the blacked-out names in a locked drawer.

Common interview traps.

  • Redacting in the app but not in the vendor SDK that auto-captures bodies.
  • Using plain SHA-256 of an email as a "safe id" (guessable by hashing a list of emails).
  • Redacting at read time (in the dashboard) rather than write time: the raw data is still stored.
  • Forgetting that reversible-token vaults are themselves PII stores needing TTL and access control.

notes.title: Retention, access and deletion for traces
notes.html:
What it is. Redaction lowers the risk; retention and access control cap the damage when redaction misses something.

Practices.

  • Tiered retention: metrics (counts, latencies) for 13 months to see year-over-year trends; redacted traces for about 30 days (a common choice; your policy and law decide); raw content for hours or not at all. These numbers are illustrative, not a standard.
  • Role-based access: most engineers see only redacted traces; a small on-call group sees more, with audit logging of every view.
  • Encrypt at rest, use region-pinned storage if the law requires data to stay in a region.
  • Deletion pathway: a "right to erasure" request must find a user's data in traces, caches, vector indexes and eval sets. That only works if every record carries the keyed user id from the previous section, so you can search and delete by it.
  • Evaluation datasets: when you copy production traces into a test set, redact again, review, and record where each example came from.
  • Vendor due diligence: data processing agreement, sub-processors, retention settings, whether the vendor trains on your data.

Real products. Langfuse and Arize Phoenix can be self-hosted so data stays in your cloud; LangSmith, Datadog LLM Observability and others offer hosted tiers with masking features (verify feature names and plans in each product's docs).

Everyday analogy. A shredder schedule for the office: paper that is not needed gets shredded on a timetable, and only a few people hold the key to the filing cabinet.

Common interview traps.

  • Keeping everything "forever for debugging". Storage you do not need is liability you do carry.
  • Deleting from the log store but not the cache that holds the same prompt.
  • Giving the whole company read access to production traces.
  • Assuming self-hosting is automatically compliant. You still own retention, access and breach duties.

notes.title: Measuring bias with counterfactual tests
notes.html:
What it is. Bias here means the model behaves differently for people or groups in ways that are unfair or unrelated to the task. Measurement means turning "it feels biased" into a number you can track.

Why it is hard. There is no single definition of fair. Equal outcomes across groups, equal error rates across groups, and ignoring the protected attribute can conflict, and you cannot satisfy all of them at once in general. So first pick the definition that fits the product, then measure it. See also in 02_S1: "Bias and fairness" for sources of bias and mitigation practices; here the focus is the measuring procedure.

The core technique: counterfactual (paired) testing. Take one prompt, change only a signal of group identity (a name, pronoun, dialect, nationality), keep everything else identical, and compare the model's behaviour. Because the pair differs in one thing, any systematic difference is attributable to that thing.

Step by step:

  1. Pick a task with a measurable outcome: hiring screen says "advance" or "reject", a loan assistant says "approve" or "decline", a support bot is "helpful" or "refuses", a sentiment score, answer length, refusal.
  2. Build base prompts (say 200) from realistic, equally qualified cases.
  3. Create variants by swapping the attribute (for example names common in group A vs group B). Keep a clean list of swaps.
  4. Run each variant several times with the same settings (temperature above zero gives noise, so repeat, say 5 runs, or set temperature 0 and note that this hides variance).
  5. Score outputs automatically (label, rule, or an LLM judge calibrated against human labels).
  6. Compute the gap and test whether it is bigger than noise.

Worked numbers. 200 matched pairs. Group A variant advanced in 124 cases, group B variant in 112.

  • Rate A = 124 / 200 = 0.62, rate B = 112 / 200 = 0.56, gap = 0.06 (6 percentage points).
  • Treating them as independent samples: standard error = sqrt(0.62 x 0.38 / 200 + 0.56 x 0.44 / 200) = sqrt(0.001178 + 0.001232) = sqrt(0.00241) = 0.0491. z = 0.06 / 0.0491 = 1.22. A z of 1.96 is the usual 95 percent bar, so this looks not significant.
  • But the data are paired, which is more powerful. Count discordant pairs (the two variants got different outcomes): A advanced and B rejected in 18 pairs (b), B advanced and A rejected in 6 pairs (c). Check: b - c = 12 matches 124 - 112 = 12. McNemar z = (b - c) / sqrt(b + c) = 12 / sqrt(24) = 12 / 4.90 = 2.45, which exceeds 1.96, so significant at about the 95 percent level.
  • Lesson: the same system can look fair or unfair depending on the test used, and with paired data you must use the paired test.

Other measures worth naming:

  • Demographic parity difference: gap in positive-outcome rate between groups (what we just computed).
  • Equal opportunity difference: gap in true positive rate among truly qualified people (needs ground truth).
  • Refusal/quality-of-service gap: does the bot refuse or answer worse in dialect B or language B? Measure refusal rate, answer length, and judged quality per slice.
  • Embedding or sentiment gap: mean sentiment of generated text about group A vs B.
  • Public benchmarks such as BBQ (question answering bias) and BOLD (open-ended generation bias) give a standard starting point; your own domain tests matter more (verify current benchmark versions).
  • The four-fifths rule used in US employment law flags concern when one group's selection rate is below 80 percent of the highest group's rate. Here 0.56 / 0.62 = 0.903, so above 0.80, but that rule of thumb is a screening heuristic and not a safe harbour; ask legal.
import math

def mcnemar_z(b: int, c: int) -> float:
    """b = A yes/B no pairs, c = B yes/A no pairs."""
    return (b - c) / math.sqrt(b + c) if b + c else 0.0

def run_pair(model, template: str, name_a: str, name_b: str) -> tuple[bool, bool]:
    # model(prompt) -> True if "advance"; swap ONLY the name
    return model(template.format(name=name_a)), model(template.format(name=name_b))

def bias_report(model, templates, name_a, name_b):
    b = c = 0
    for t in templates:
        a_ok, b_ok = run_pair(model, t, name_a, name_b)
        b += a_ok and not b_ok
        c += b_ok and not a_ok
    return {"b": b, "c": c, "z": mcnemar_z(b, c)}   # |z| > 1.96 -> investigate

print(mcnemar_z(18, 6))  # about 2.45
import kotlin.math.sqrt

fun mcnemarZ(b: Int, c: Int): Double = if (b + c == 0) 0.0 else (b - c) / sqrt((b + c).toDouble())

// model: (prompt) -> true when the outcome is "advance"
fun biasReport(model: (String) -> Boolean, templates: List<String>, nameA: String, nameB: String): Map<String, Number> {
    var b = 0
    var c = 0
    for (t in templates) {
        val a = model(t.replace("{name}", nameA))
        val bb = model(t.replace("{name}", nameB))
        if (a && !bb) b++
        if (bb && !a) c++
    }
    return mapOf("b" to b, "c" to c, "z" to mcnemarZ(b, c))   // |z| > 1.96 -> investigate
}
// mcnemarZ(18, 6) is about 2.45
import java.util.List;
import java.util.function.Predicate;

public class BiasTest {
    static double mcnemarZ(int b, int c) {
        return (b + c == 0) ? 0.0 : (b - c) / Math.sqrt(b + c);
    }

    /** model returns true when the outcome is "advance". Returns {b, c, z}. */
    static double[] report(Predicate<String> model, List<String> templates, String nameA, String nameB) {
        int b = 0, c = 0;
        for (String t : templates) {
            boolean a = model.test(t.replace("{name}", nameA));
            boolean bb = model.test(t.replace("{name}", nameB));
            if (a && !bb) b++;
            if (bb && !a) c++;
        }
        return new double[] { b, c, mcnemarZ(b, c) };   // |z| > 1.96 -> investigate
    }
    // mcnemarZ(18, 6) is about 2.45
}

Real products and studies. Studies of resume screening with swapped names have found models preferring some groups (published research on this exists; verify the specific papers before citing). Image generators have been caught producing skewed professions, which is how many vendors first learned to test representation. Toxicity detectors have been shown to over-flag African-American English, an example of a quality-of-service gap.

Everyday analogy. Sending two identical CVs that differ only by name to the same employer, as audit-study researchers do, and counting call-backs.

Common interview traps.

  • Reporting a gap without a significance test or confidence interval (or using an unpaired test on paired data).
  • Testing only names. Dialect, language, disability mentions, age, location and gendered terms all matter.
  • Assuming "remove the protected attribute from the prompt" fixes bias. Proxies (zip code, school, hobbies) carry the signal.
  • Using the LLM judge to score bias without checking that the judge is itself unbiased.

notes.title: Bias in production: slices, sampling and mitigation loop
notes.html:
What it is. A one-off bias test before launch decays. Models are updated by the vendor, prompts change, user mix shifts. Treat bias like a regression test plus a live metric.

Practices.

  1. Put the counterfactual suite in CI so every prompt or model change reruns it. Gate releases on "no new significant gap" and "no worse than baseline by more than a set margin".
  2. Define slices you can legally and ethically measure: language, locale, device type, plan tier, and (only where lawful and with consent) self-reported demographics. You often cannot measure a protected attribute directly in production, so you use proxies or opt-in surveys, and you say so in documentation.
  3. Track slice metrics: refusal rate, escalation rate, thumbs-down rate, average judged quality, latency. A drop in one slice that is hidden inside a healthy global average is the classic miss. Example: global refusal is 3 percent, but for Hindi-language queries 9 percent. Weighted: if Hindi is 10 percent of traffic, the rest is 90 percent and refusal there is (3 - 0.9) / 0.9 = 2.33 percent, so the average hid a nearly 4 times gap.
  4. Mitigations, cheapest first: fix the prompt (clear rubric, instructions to base the decision on listed criteria only), balance few-shot examples, mask names or other identity cues before the model sees the case, calibrate thresholds, add human review for consequential decisions, and for high stakes keep the model advisory only.
  5. Close the loop: provide an appeal or feedback path, review complaints, and add each real failure to the test suite.
  6. Document: a model card or system card, the known limitations, the tests run and when.

Real products. Hiring-tech vendors have faced regulation requiring bias audits for automated employment tools in some jurisdictions (for example New York City's rule on automated employment decision tools; verify current status). The EU AI Act classes employment and credit scoring uses as high risk with documentation and oversight duties (verify scope and dates).

Everyday analogy. A school that tracks results by class and neighbourhood every term instead of only looking at the school-wide average.

Common interview traps.

  • Optimising the global average and missing a failing slice.
  • Saying "we don't collect demographics so we can't be biased". Not measuring is not the same as not being biased.
  • Fixing a failure by hard-coding the exact failing example. Fix the cause, then add the case to the suite.
  • Letting the model make the final high-stakes decision with no human or appeal path.

notes.title: Content safety: detecting harmful outputs
notes.html:
What it is. Content safety is detecting text (and images, audio) that is harmful: hate, harassment, sexual content, violence, self-harm, illegal activity, dangerous instructions, and also brand-specific "not allowed" content (medical advice from a retail bot).

Why. Even with a safety-trained model, harmful output can appear through jailbreaks, ambiguous prompts, retrieved content, or role-play. Providers train models to refuse, but your product has its own policy, and defence needs more than one layer.

Detection approaches.

Approach How Strength Weakness
Keyword/regex lists match known bad terms fast, explainable misses paraphrase, flags innocent text ("Scunthorpe problem")
Trained classifier small model gives scores per category fast, tunable threshold needs data, weaker on new attacks
LLM-as-judge prompt a model with your policy flexible, reads context slower, costlier, variable, can be attacked
Moderation API provider's hosted classifier no training, maintained fixed categories, data leaves your system
Human review sample or escalate highest accuracy slow, costly, reviewer wellbeing

How classifier-based filtering works step by step.

  1. The classifier returns a score between 0 and 1 for each category.
  2. You choose a threshold per category. Lower threshold means more blocks (higher recall, more false positives); higher means fewer blocks.
  3. Three zones: score above block threshold -> refuse; between review and block thresholds -> allow but log for human review, or ask the user to rephrase; below -> allow.
  4. Calibrate on a labelled set from your own traffic. Measure precision (of those blocked, how many truly bad) and recall (of the truly bad, how many blocked).

Worked threshold example. Suppose 10,000 outputs, 100 truly harmful (1 percent). At threshold 0.5 the classifier catches 80 of them (recall 80 percent) and wrongly blocks 120 harmless ones. Precision = 80 / (80 + 120) = 40 percent. At threshold 0.8 it catches 60 (recall 60 percent) and wrongly blocks 20. Precision = 60 / 80 = 75 percent. Which is right depends on harm: for a children's app choose 0.5 and accept annoyed users; for a medical-research tool choose 0.8 plus human review.

Context matters. The same sentence is fine in a crime-novel writing tool and not fine in a kids' tutor. Per-product policy, per-category thresholds and a system prompt describing the audience are normal.

Special cases to name.

  • Self-harm: do not just refuse; respond with supportive text and crisis resources, per safety guidance for your region.
  • Images and multimodal: images can carry text instructions or unsafe content, so use image moderation too.
  • Agents: harmful action matters more than harmful words, so action filters and human approval come first.
  • Streaming: see the output validation section.
import json, os
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment
POLICY = "Label the text SAFE or UNSAFE. UNSAFE = hate, self-harm instructions, violence incitement, or sexual content involving minors. Reply with JSON only: {\"label\":\"SAFE|UNSAFE\",\"category\":\"...\"}"

def classify(text: str) -> dict:
    msg = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-haiku-5-5",   # verify current model id
        max_tokens=60,
        system=POLICY,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": f"<text>\n{text}\n</text>"}],
    )
    try:
        out = json.loads(msg.content[0].text)
        return out if out.get("label") in ("SAFE", "UNSAFE") else {"label": "UNSAFE", "category": "PARSE"}
    except (json.JSONDecodeError, IndexError):
        return {"label": "UNSAFE", "category": "PARSE"}   # fail closed

print(classify("How do I bake bread?"))  # {'label': 'SAFE', 'category': 'none'}
import com.anthropic.client.okhttp.AnthropicOkHttpClient
import com.anthropic.models.messages.MessageCreateParams
import kotlinx.serialization.json.*

val client = AnthropicOkHttpClient.fromEnv()   // ANTHROPIC_API_KEY; verify builder names in the SDK docs
const val POLICY = "Label the text SAFE or UNSAFE. Reply with JSON only: {\"label\":\"SAFE|UNSAFE\",\"category\":\"...\"}"

fun classify(text: String): String {
    val params = MessageCreateParams.builder()
        .model("claude-haiku-5-5")          // verify current model id
        .maxTokens(60)
        .system(POLICY)
        .addUserMessage("<text>\n$text\n</text>")
        .build()
    val reply = client.messages().create(params).content()
        .firstOrNull()?.text()?.get()?.text() ?: return "UNSAFE"   // verify accessor names
    return try {
        Json.parseToJsonElement(reply).jsonObject["label"]?.jsonPrimitive?.content ?: "UNSAFE"
    } catch (e: Exception) { "UNSAFE" }   // fail closed
}
import com.anthropic.client.AnthropicClient;
import com.anthropic.client.okhttp.AnthropicOkHttpClient;
import com.anthropic.models.messages.*;

public class ContentSafety {
    static final AnthropicClient CLIENT = AnthropicOkHttpClient.fromEnv(); // ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
    static final String POLICY = "Label the text SAFE or UNSAFE. Reply with JSON only: {\"label\":\"SAFE|UNSAFE\",\"category\":\"...\"}";

    static boolean isSafe(String text) {
        try {
            MessageCreateParams p = MessageCreateParams.builder()
                .model("claude-haiku-5-5")      // verify current model id
                .maxTokens(60)
                .system(POLICY)
                .addUserMessage("<text>\n" + text + "\n</text>")
                .build();
            Message m = CLIENT.messages().create(p);
            String out = m.content().get(0).asText().text();   // verify accessor names in the SDK docs
            return out.contains("\"SAFE\"") && !out.contains("UNSAFE");
        } catch (Exception e) {
            return false;   // fail closed
        }
    }
}

Key design points in the snippets: the judge only returns a label (small, parseable), parse failure counts as UNSAFE (fail closed), and the text is wrapped in tags so it is treated as data. A cheap fast model keeps latency low; budget about one extra model call per message, so cost and latency rise (verify prices).

Real products. OpenAI Moderation, Llama Guard, ShieldGemma (Google), Azure AI Content Safety and Amazon Bedrock Guardrails content filters (verify category lists and availability), plus Perspective API for toxicity (verify whether it is still offered).

Everyday analogy. A film ratings board that sorts a film into G, PG or R and a cinema that decides what to show to which audience.

Common interview traps.

  • Using one global threshold for all categories and audiences.
  • Reporting only accuracy. With 1 percent bad content, "always say safe" is 99 percent accurate, so use precision and recall.
  • Having no escape for false positives: users need a way to rephrase or appeal, and you need to log blocked cases to find over-blocking.
  • Using the same prompt-injectable model as both generator and judge without isolating the judged text.

notes.title: Monitoring GenAI systems in production
notes.html:
What it is. Monitoring means continuously measuring the live system so you know when it is unhealthy. Classic services have well-known signals (errors, latency). GenAI adds a failure that raises no exception: the system returns HTTP 200 with a confident but wrong or unsafe answer. So you need quality and safety signals on top of the usual ones.

The four groups of signals.

1 RELIABILITY   request rate, error rate (4xx/5xx/429), timeouts, retries
2 PERFORMANCE   latency p50/p95/p99, time to first token, tokens per second
3 COST          input tokens, output tokens, cache hit rate, cost per request/user
4 QUALITY+SAFETY
                filter block rate by reason code, moderation flags, refusal rate,
                JSON/schema failure rate, tool error rate, groundedness score,
                thumbs-down rate, escalation to human, drift in input mix

Why each matters, with a failure each catches.

  • Error rate and 429s: provider rate limit or outage. Fix: retry with backoff, fall back to another model.
  • Latency percentiles: averages hide the slow tail. If 5 percent of requests take 30 seconds the mean looks fine. Alert on p95/p99.
  • Tokens and cost: a prompt change that adds 500 tokens to every request multiplies spend; a loop in an agent burns money. Example: 1 million requests a day x 500 extra input tokens = 500 million extra tokens a day; at an illustrative 3 dollars per million input tokens (verify real prices) that is 1,500 dollars a day extra.
  • Block rate by reason: a jump in INJECTION_PATTERN means an attack campaign or a broken regex; a drop to zero means the filter is silently disabled.
  • Schema failure rate: the vendor updated the model and now wraps JSON in prose.
  • Refusal rate: up means over-blocking or a model update that got stricter; down might mean a safety layer broke.
  • Quality sampling: automatically score a small sample (for example 1 to 5 percent) of live traffic with an LLM judge or rules, and track the score as a time series. Drift detection compares this week's input distribution (topics, languages, length) with a baseline.
  • User feedback: thumbs-down rate and "regenerate" clicks are cheap, honest quality signals.

Instrumentation. Emit a metric at every filter decision and a span per model call. Use low-cardinality labels (reason code, model id, route) on metrics; keep high-cardinality things (user id, prompt) out of metric labels because each unique label value creates a new time series and can overwhelm the metrics backend. Put request ids on logs and traces so you can jump from an alert to a trace.

Dashboards. One page per service: traffic, errors, latency percentiles, cost, then a safety panel (blocks by reason, refusals, flagged outputs) and a quality panel (judge score, thumbs-down, slice metrics from the bias section). Mark deploy times and prompt versions on the graphs so a change correlates with a jump.

Real products. Prometheus plus Grafana, Datadog, New Relic and OpenTelemetry for the metrics layer; Langfuse, LangSmith, Arize, Helicone, WhyLabs and similar for LLM-specific traces and evals (verify current product lineups).

Everyday analogy. A car dashboard. Speed (latency), fuel (cost), engine warning light (errors), and, new for GenAI, a check-the-passenger light that tells you the driver is steering confidently into a wall even though the engine is fine.

Common interview traps.

  • Monitoring only infrastructure health. A fully green dashboard with wrong answers is the GenAI default failure.
  • Using averages for latency and cost.
  • High-cardinality metric labels (user id, session id, raw prompt text).
  • Not versioning prompts, so you cannot say which prompt version caused the regression.

notes.title: Alerts that people act on
notes.html:
What it is. An alert is a rule that pages or messages a human when a metric crosses a line. The goal is the right person is told about a real problem quickly, and not woken for noise.

Principles.

  1. Alert on symptoms users feel (error rate, block rate spike, latency, cost burn), not on every cause.
  2. Every page has a runbook link: what the alert means, how to check, how to mitigate, who to call.
  3. Use windows and minimum volume. A single blocked request out of two is 50 percent, which means nothing. Require at least N requests in the window.
  4. Compare to a baseline, not only a fixed number, when traffic is seasonal.
  5. Severity levels: page for user harm now (secret leak, harmful output flagged, outage), ticket for slow burn (drift, rising cost).
  6. Tune after each incident. Alert fatigue (people ignore a channel that cries wolf) is a bigger risk than a missing alert.

Worked sizing example. Normal block rate is 2 percent. You want to catch a jump to 6 percent (3 times baseline). In a 15 minute window with 100 requests, the expected block count at 2 percent is 2, and the standard deviation of the rate is sqrt(0.02 x 0.98 / 100) = sqrt(0.000196) = 0.014, i.e. 1.4 points. A 6 percent reading is (0.06 - 0.02) / 0.014 = 2.9 standard deviations above normal, which is rare by chance (roughly 0.2 percent one-sided), so alerting at 3 times baseline with at least 100 requests keeps false pages low. With only 20 requests the standard deviation is sqrt(0.0196 / 20) = 0.031, and 6 percent is only 1.3 deviations, which is common noise, hence the minimum-volume rule.

Error-budget (burn rate) alerts. If your SLO (service level objective) says 99.5 percent of requests succeed over 30 days, the error budget is 0.5 percent of requests. A burn rate of 1 means you consume the budget exactly over 30 days. A burn rate of 14.4 over 1 hour would use 2 percent of the monthly budget in that hour (14.4 x 1 hour / 720 hours = 0.02) and deserves a page; this multi-window pattern is described in Google's SRE workbook (verify exact numbers there).

Safety-specific alerts.

  • Any SECRET_LEAK or a trace containing an unredacted PII pattern: page immediately (counts, not rates).
  • Spike in flagged-harmful outputs or in INJECTION_PATTERN.
  • Block rate dropping to zero (filter off), or filter timeout rate rising (filter failing open).
  • Refusal rate change after a model or prompt deploy.
  • Cost per user above a ceiling (abuse or a loop).
  • Slice metric gap exceeding a bound (bias section).

Response flow. Alert -> acknowledge -> use request id to open a redacted trace -> mitigate first (roll back the prompt, switch the model route, tighten a threshold, disable a tool, enable a kill switch) -> investigate -> write a post-incident review -> add a test or alert so it cannot recur silently. See also in 02_S1: "Incident response" for the security-incident side.

from collections import deque
import time

class RateAlert:
    """Alert when block rate over a sliding window exceeds `ratio` x baseline, with minimum volume."""
    def __init__(self, baseline=0.02, ratio=3.0, window_s=900, min_n=100):
        self.baseline, self.ratio, self.window_s, self.min_n = baseline, ratio, window_s, min_n
        self.events = deque()  # (timestamp, blocked: bool)

    def record(self, blocked: bool, now=None) -> bool:
        now = now or time.time()
        self.events.append((now, blocked))
        while self.events and self.events[0][0] < now - self.window_s:
            self.events.popleft()
        n = len(self.events)
        if n < self.min_n:
            return False
        rate = sum(b for _, b in self.events) / n
        return rate >= self.baseline * self.ratio   # True -> fire alert

a = RateAlert()
fired = [a.record(i % 12 == 0, now=i) for i in range(200)]   # about 8.3 percent blocked
print(fired[-1])  # True
import java.util.ArrayDeque

class RateAlert(
    private val baseline: Double = 0.02,
    private val ratio: Double = 3.0,
    private val windowMs: Long = 900_000,
    private val minN: Int = 100,
) {
    private data class Ev(val ts: Long, val blocked: Boolean)
    private val events = ArrayDeque<Ev>()

    /** Returns true when the alert should fire. */
    @Synchronized
    fun record(blocked: Boolean, now: Long = System.currentTimeMillis()): Boolean {
        events.addLast(Ev(now, blocked))
        while (events.isNotEmpty() && events.first().ts < now - windowMs) events.removeFirst()
        if (events.size < minN) return false
        val rate = events.count { it.blocked }.toDouble() / events.size
        return rate >= baseline * ratio
    }
}
import java.util.ArrayDeque;

public class RateAlert {
    private record Ev(long ts, boolean blocked) {}
    private final ArrayDeque<Ev> events = new ArrayDeque<>();
    private final double baseline, ratio;
    private final long windowMs;
    private final int minN;

    public RateAlert(double baseline, double ratio, long windowMs, int minN) {
        this.baseline = baseline; this.ratio = ratio; this.windowMs = windowMs; this.minN = minN;
    }

    /** Returns true when the alert should fire. */
    public synchronized boolean record(boolean blocked, long now) {
        events.addLast(new Ev(now, blocked));
        while (!events.isEmpty() && events.peekFirst().ts() < now - windowMs) events.removeFirst();
        if (events.size() < minN) return false;
        long bad = events.stream().filter(Ev::blocked).count();
        return (double) bad / events.size() >= baseline * ratio;
    }
}

In production you rarely hand-roll this: you emit counters (Prometheus, Datadog, OTel metrics) and write the rule in the alerting system (for example a PromQL rate ratio over 15 minutes). The class above shows the logic and is useful for in-process circuit breakers (for example automatically tightening a filter).

Everyday analogy. A smoke detector tuned so that burnt toast does not wake the whole building but a real fire does, with a card on the wall telling you which exit to use.

Common interview traps.

  • Alerting on a rate without a minimum request count.
  • Static thresholds only, causing false alarms at night when traffic is low.
  • Alerts with no runbook or owner, so the page is ignored.
  • Having no kill switch or rollback for prompts and tools, so detection does not lead to mitigation.

notes.title: How the pieces fit together in one request
notes.html:
What it is. A single walk-through tying the five topics together, as you could explain it in an interview whiteboard round.

Scenario. An Android banking assistant. The app calls your own backend (never ship the model API key in the APK), the backend calls the model.

Android app --HTTPS--> backend /chat
  1. auth, per-user rate limit
  2. validate_input    -> reason code? count metric block{reason}
  3. redact for model? (card numbers masked before leaving your cloud)
  4. retrieve context (only this user's data: tenant filter)
  5. model call (span: tokens, latency, model id, prompt version)
  6. validate_output   -> schema, secrets, PII, harm classifier
  7. action filter     -> allow-list, amount limits, human approval for transfers
  8. respond to app
  9. trace written AFTER redact(); user id as HMAC key; content sampled 1%
 10. nightly job: counterfactual bias suite on current prompt+model; slice metrics
 11. alert rules on block rate, refusal rate, cost, secret leak, latency p95

Why each step: steps 2 and 6 are the safety filters; 3 and 9 keep PII out of vendor and trace stores; 10 measures bias continuously; 11 turns metrics into action. The Android client itself only displays text; it must still escape output, avoid Log.d of prompts, and avoid putting content into crash-report keys.

Cost and latency budget. Input regex ~1 ms, redaction ~1 to 5 ms, moderation call ~100 to 300 ms (verify), main model 1 to 5 s. Run the input moderation call in parallel with the main model call and cancel the model call if moderation blocks; this hides most of the moderation latency at the cost of occasionally paying for a call you discard.

Trade-offs to state. More filters means more latency, more cost and more false positives; fewer filters means more risk. Choose by harm severity: a trivia bot needs light filters, a banking or health assistant needs strict ones plus humans in the loop.

Everyday analogy. A restaurant kitchen: the order is checked at the till (input), the chef cooks, the pass inspects every plate (output), allergens are labelled (PII/action rules), the health inspector reads the logs (monitoring), and the manager reviews complaints by table type (bias slices).

Common interview traps.

  • Describing filters without saying where PII goes in the logs.
  • Forgetting the Android client side: no API key in the app, no sensitive prompt logging, escaped rendering.
  • Saying parallel moderation is free. You may pay for model tokens you throw away.
  • Skipping the answer to "how would you know it broke?" which is the monitoring section.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Safety is a stack of cheap, ordered filters: input, output, action and trace. Decide fail-open or fail-closed for each, return reason codes, and measure false positives and false negatives. No stack reaches zero risk.
  • Validate inputs for size, Unicode tricks, injection phrases and PII. Validate outputs for schema, secrets, PII, harm and safe rendering. The model proposes, your allow-listed code disposes.
  • Traces are PII stores. Prefer logging metadata over content, sample and redact content at write time, use keyed hashes (HMAC) not plain hashes, tier retention, restrict access, and make deletion by user key possible.
  • Measure bias with counterfactual pairs: change one identity signal, keep the rest fixed, compare outcomes, and use the right statistical test (paired data needs McNemar, for example z = 12 / sqrt(24) = 2.45). Track slices continuously, because a healthy average can hide a failing group.
  • Detect harmful content with layered methods (rules, classifiers, LLM judges, moderation APIs, humans). Tune thresholds per category and audience, judge by precision and recall, and fail closed on parse errors.
  • Monitor reliability, latency percentiles, cost, and quality and safety signals. Silent wrong answers return HTTP 200, so sample and score live traffic and watch filter block rates by reason.
  • Alert on user-visible symptoms with minimum volumes, baselines, burn rates and runbooks; keep a kill switch and rollback ready. Fast-moving details (model ids, prices, product features, regulation scope) are marked verify and must be checked against current docs.
